Among the many ironies of modern travel, one deserves particular attention: the places most worth seeing are often the ones most endangered by those who come to see them. When crowds fill the narrow lanes of a historic city such as Venice, it is natural (12)______. Closer inspection often tells a different story. A large number of the apartments along its canals are, in fact, holiday homes (13)______, while the families who once lived there have moved to the mainland. The historic centre now has fewer than 50,000 residents, and tourist beds outnumber local people. (14)______.

We tend to judge a destination's health by what we can see, as busy streets are the only evidence most visitors have access to. Nobody stepping off a train is handed a record of how many neighbours have left, (15)______ – packed squares, full restaurants, queues at every bridge – to conclude that the city is flourishing. Tourism marketing has fed this habit, packaging the crowd itself as proof of success. (16)______. It lies in the corner shop that stays open, the school that keeps its pupils and the neighbour who can still afford to stay.

In short, a city is more than the number of people who pass through it. Venice's decision in 2024 to test a €5 entry fee for day-trippers shows that some places are already searching for a better balance. That is why distinguishing busy from alive deserves careful thought; mistaking one for the other has quietly emptied many a historic centre.

For most of human history, the night sky was a shared inheritance: a dark canopy of stars that guided travellers, farmers and sailors alike. Today, that inheritance is vanishing. Light pollution – artificial light that spills beyond the places it is meant to illuminate – has become so

that a large share of the world's population can no longer see the Milky Way from their own homes. Unlike many environmental problems, it leaves behind no chemical waste, only brightness, and because brightness seems harmless, its consequences have long gone unnoticed.

The consequences for wildlife are the best documented. Birds that migrate at night rely on the moon and stars to find their way, yet many are drawn towards brightly lit towers and skyscrapers, circling until they are exhausted or colliding with the glass. Young birds on their first journey suffer disproportionately. On beaches, newly hatched sea turtles instinctively crawl towards the brightest horizon, which in nature is the sea reflecting the sky; street lamps and hotels behind the beach now compete with it, and hatchlings that head inland seldom survive. Even animals that are not harmed directly are affected: some nocturnal mammals forage more cautiously under artificial light because it makes them easier targets for predators.
Humans are not immune. Our bodies, too, run on an internal clock tuned to the daily cycle of light and darkness.
Bright light late at night can suppress the production of melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate sleep.
Researchers have linked chronic sleep disruption to a range of health problems, from poor concentration to a higher risk of heart disease.
Some scientists suspect that night-shift workers, who spend long hours under bright lighting, may be especially at risk.
Yet because artificial light feels like a convenience rather than a hazard, few people connect their restless nights with the glow outside their windows.

The encouraging news is that light pollution is among the easiest environmental problems to solve. Nothing has to be cleaned up; the light simply has to be directed where it is needed. A growing number of towns have created "dark-sky" zones in which outdoor lights must be shielded and dimmed late at night.
have found that such measures save energy while still keeping their streets lit where light is needed. The danger lies not in lighting our streets, but in lighting them thoughtlessly.

Ask almost anyone where good ideas come from, and the answer usually involves a quiet room, a desk and a long stretch of uninterrupted sitting. Generations of students and office workers have been taught that real thinking requires stillness, and that a wandering body leads to a wandering mind. Yet few people stop to ask whether this belief rests on evidence or merely on habit.

Researchers at Stanford University set out to test it. In a series of experiments involving 176 participants, they asked people to think up unusual uses for everyday objects, once while sitting and once while walking. On average, participants came up with about 60 percent more creative ideas while walking than
The boost came from walking itself rather than from the scenery, since people on an indoor treadmill facing a blank wall benefited as well

Why should putting one foot in front of the other loosen the mind? The exact mechanism remains unclear, but one plausible explanation is that walking lifts mood and energy while freeing attention from the pressure to produce an answer at once. This relaxed state may be

to divergent thinking, which psychologists define as the ability to generate many possible solutions to an open-ended question. Remarkably, the benefit did not vanish the moment the walk ended: participants who sat down again shortly afterwards continued to show higher creativity.

None of this means that a walk is a cure-all. The same studies found no comparable gain on tasks that demand a single correct answer, so anyone hoping that a stroll will solve every intellectual problem is likely to be disappointed. Moreover, because the experiments were short and carried out largely in laboratory conditions, the findings remain
. The sensible conclusion is not that desks should be abandoned, but that different kinds of thinking may call for different conditions.
